clue.text: Small biting insect bit

blocks.note: S is the standard abbreviation for small, as on clothing labels
a midge is a tiny insect that bites

explanation.surface: Someone has been nipped by a tiny insect while out walking.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bit' looks like the past tense of bite, continuing the insect story, but it is a noun meaning a small amount.
explanation.definitionFit: A smidge is a colloquial term for a tiny quantity, just as a bit is.

clue.text: Mum queueing here for the fast train

definitions.note: a place description: the main line is where the fast trains run

blocks.note: Ma is an informal word for mother
people queueing are standing in line

explanation.surface: A mother stands in the queue at the station waiting to board the express.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is descriptive rather than a strict synonym: the main line is the principal railway route, the one served by fast trains.
explanation.definitionFit: On a railway the main line is the trunk route carrying express services, as opposed to slower branch lines.

clue.text: Harangue clan after help rejected

indicators.note: something rejected is sent back, so this down-light word is read in the opposite direction
the word before 'after' is placed following the other piece, fixing their order

blocks.note: aid is a synonym of help; it is turned round to DIA
a clan is a tribe, a kinship group

explanation.surface: An angry rant directed at a family group whose offer of help was turned down.
explanation.definitionFit: A diatribe is a bitter verbal attack, the same thing as a harangue.

clue.text: The French No.1 book is flipping hot-blooded!

indicators.note: flipping something turns it over, so the whole string of pieces is read backwards

blocks.note: la is a French word for 'the' (feminine)
No. is the abbreviation for number, and 1 is the Roman numeral I
a tome is a large book

explanation.surface: An exasperated cry that a French bestseller is a passionate read.
explanation.walkthrough: 'flipping' poses as a mild British expletive, but it reverses LANOITOME as a whole.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone hot-blooded is passionate and easily roused, which is to say emotional.

clue.text: Heavenly place is seen in March

indicators.note: something seen in another thing sits within it, so one word goes inside the other

blocks.note: taken as written
a march is a parade; the IS goes before its last letter

explanation.surface: A claim that spring weather in the third month of the year is heavenly.
explanation.walkthrough: March reads as the month because of its capital, but it is the verb-turned-noun for a procession.
explanation.definitionFit: Paradise is the dwelling of the blessed, heaven itself.

clue.text: Eh? Aren't down t'pit working? Get partying!

indicators.note: the miners are 'not working' in the surface, but working here means the letters are worked into a new order

blocks.note: the fifteen letters of these words are rearranged

explanation.surface: A Northern miner, surprised to find no shift down the pit, decides to go out and celebrate.
explanation.walkthrough: 't'pit' is Yorkshire dialect for 'the pit', the coal mine. The definition is an imperative, matching the idiom used as a command.
explanation.definitionFit: To paint the town red is an idiom for going out and celebrating wildly, exactly what partying means.

clue.text: Husband enters – humbled, embarrassed

indicators.note: a letter that enters a word goes inside it, so it is placed within the other piece

blocks.note: H is the abbreviation for husband
abased means humbled or brought low; the H goes after ABAS

explanation.surface: A husband walks in feeling humiliated and red-faced.
explanation.definitionFit: Abashed describes someone disconcerted and ashamed, which is what embarrassed means.

clue.text: Problem for those who can't close lids satisfactorily?

definitions.text: Problem for those who can't close lids satisfactorily?

blocks.clueFragment: Problem for those who can't close lids satisfactorily?
blocks.note: surface reading: a difficulty with jars, boxes or containers whose lids won't shut
setter's reading: the lids are eyelids, and someone who cannot properly shut their eyes cannot sleep

explanation.walkthrough: The lids look like those of pots or bins; they are eyelids, and the problem is a sleep disorder.
explanation.definitionFit: Insomnia is chronic inability to fall or stay asleep, the plight of someone whose eyes will not stay closed.

clue.text: A bit of horticulture? Yep, at Chelsea covering for The Observer

indicators.note: a bit of a word is just one of its letters, here the closing one
the run of words covers the answer's remaining letters, holding them across the word gaps

blocks.note: the final letter of horticulture
the letters run consecutively through Yep, at and the start of Chelsea

explanation.surface: A gardening question at the Chelsea Flower Show, answered with a casual 'yep', reported for a Sunday newspaper.
explanation.walkthrough: The Observer looks like the British Sunday newspaper, but it is anyone who observes, i.e. uses their eyes. 'covering' does double duty, also starting the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: An eyepatch is a cover worn over one eye, so it is a covering for someone who looks or watches.

clue.text: Italian tubes inside parts of frigate won't fit

indicators.note: the inside parts of words are their interiors, so the first and last letters are dropped from each

blocks.note: frigate without its outer letters
the interior of won't, apostrophe ignored
the middle letter of fit

explanation.surface: Some pasta tubes are being forced into the compartments of a warship and will not go.
explanation.definitionFit: Rigatoni is a pasta shaped into short, ridged tubes, from Italy.

clue.text: Film star of the Forties even more stylish when undressed

indicators.note: undressing strips away the outer layer, so the first and last letters go

blocks.note: classier means more stylish; its inner letters are kept

explanation.surface: An actress of 1940s Hollywood looked even more glamorous without her clothes.
explanation.walkthrough: The star is not a human actress but the collie dog who first appeared in Lassie Come Home (1943).
explanation.definitionFit: Lassie, the fictional collie, starred in a run of MGM films in the 1940s.

clue.text: Easily scared top celebs packing gun?

indicators.note: a person packing a weapon carries it on them, so one piece is held inside the other

blocks.note: the A-list is the top tier of celebrities; the next piece goes after AL
an arm is a weapon, a firearm

explanation.surface: Wondering whether nervous celebrities are carrying firearms for protection.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition is adjectival, but alarmist is a noun or adjective; as an adjective it describes someone quick to raise fears.
explanation.definitionFit: An alarmist person panics readily and spreads fear, so is easily scared.

clue.text: Dance, or hum Bacharach covers

indicators.note: the phrase covers, or contains, the answer within its letters spanning word gaps

blocks.note: the letters run from the end of 'or' through 'hum' into 'Bacharach'

explanation.surface: A suggestion to either dance or hum along to cover versions of Burt Bacharach songs.
explanation.walkthrough: Burt Bacharach was an American songwriter; 'covers' poses as cover versions of his songs.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhumba (rumba) is a Cuban ballroom dance.

clue.text: D'oh! Been a daft lummox

indicators.note: something daft is crazy or muddled, so the letters are jumbled

blocks.note: the eight letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Homer Simpson's catchphrase as someone admits having been a clumsy fool.
explanation.definitionFit: A bonehead is a stupid person, and a lummox is a clumsy, stupid one.

clue.text: He's bald, no flowing hair like this

indicators.note: flowing suggests loose movement, so the letters are rearranged freely

blocks.note: the nine letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A bald man insists he has no long, flowing locks.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition refers back to the answer itself: 'hair like this' describes the colour named.
explanation.definitionFit: Ash blonde is a pale, greyish shade of fair hair.

clue.text: McEnroe periodically missed in pool

indicators.note: letters missed at regular periods means every other one is dropped

blocks.note: the first, third, fifth and seventh letters

explanation.surface: The tennis star John McEnroe occasionally missed shots into a swimming pool.
explanation.definitionFit: A mere is a lake or pond, a poetic or regional word for a still body of water.

clue.text: Regulars in amiable, cheap bars here in the Indian Ocean

indicators.note: regular letters are taken at an even spacing, every second one

blocks.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters
a dive is a seedy, low-class bar

explanation.surface: A tourist's description of friendly locals in budget bars at an island resort.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Regulars' suggests bar regulars, the customers, but it selects letters.
explanation.definitionFit: The Maldives is an island nation in the Indian Ocean, the place indicated by 'here'.

clue.text: Letter to specialist concerning tiger finally captured in wild

indicators.note: finally points to the closing letter of the preceding word
something captured in a place is held inside it

blocks.note: re means about or concerning
feral means wild, untamed
the last letter of tiger, placed after FER

explanation.surface: Correspondence to an expert about a tiger caught in the wild.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a GP writes a letter of referral to send a patient to a hospital specialist.
explanation.definitionFit: A referral is a doctor's letter passing a patient on to a specialist consultant.

clue.text: Liquid asset banks from Athens deposited in Switzerland

indicators.note: the banks of a river are its edges, so the outer letters are kept
money deposited in an account is put inside it, so one piece sits within the other

blocks.note: CH is the international vehicle code for Switzerland; it wraps the next piece
the first and last letters of Athens

explanation.surface: Money from Greek banks being lodged in Swiss accounts.
explanation.walkthrough: CH stands for Confoederatio Helvetica, Switzerland's Latin name.
explanation.definitionFit: Cash is the most liquid asset, money immediately available to spend.

clue.text: Impolite when breaking wind – this needs refining

indicators.note: something breaking into another goes inside it, splitting it apart

blocks.note: to wind is to coil; this piece is split after its first letter
rude means impolite

explanation.surface: Breaking wind is rude behaviour, and the person doing it needs some refinement.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaking wind' reads as flatulence; here wind is the verb, coil.
explanation.definitionFit: Crude oil is unprocessed petroleum that must be refined into fuels.

clue.text: Deputy Governor initially running for election

indicators.note: initially points to the opening letter of the word before it

blocks.note: a stand-in is a deputy or substitute
the first letter of Governor

explanation.surface: A deputy governor is the first to put themselves forward in an election.
explanation.walkthrough: In British usage a candidate stands for election where Americans say runs.
explanation.definitionFit: Standing, in the British sense, is offering yourself as a candidate, the equivalent of running for office.

clue.text: Maker of arrows for one Christian

blocks.note: first meaning: a craftsman who makes arrows
second meaning: the first name of a famous man surnamed Christian

explanation.surface: A churchgoer who earns a living making arrows.
explanation.walkthrough: Christian is a surname here, not a believer: Fletcher Christian led the mutiny on HMS Bounty in 1789.
explanation.definitionFit: A fletcher is an arrow-maker by trade, and Fletcher Christian is the Bounty mutineer, one person called Christian.

clue.text: Dissident group following battle

blocks.note: f. is the abbreviation for following, as in page references
action is military combat, a battle

explanation.surface: A breakaway group forming in the aftermath of a battle.
explanation.definitionFit: A faction is a dissenting group within a larger body, such as a party.

clue.text: Runs into M, recently retired soak

indicators.note: one thing running into another ends up inside it

blocks.note: Dame Judi Dench played M in the James Bond films and has stepped back from acting; the next piece goes after D
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs

explanation.surface: A recently retired spy chief gets caught in a downpour while out running.
explanation.walkthrough: M is the head of MI6 in the Bond films, a role Judi Dench played from 1995 to 2015.
explanation.definitionFit: To drench is to soak something thoroughly with liquid.

clue.text: Far from rare congratulatory message

blocks.note: first meaning: cooked right through, describing a steak at the opposite end from rare
second meaning: an exclamation of praise for an achievement

explanation.walkthrough: 'Far from rare' suggests common, but rare is a steak doneness.
explanation.definitionFit: A steak cooked fully through is the opposite of rare, and the same phrase is said to praise someone's success.

clue.text: Very Young British Artist keeping river rats?

definitions.note: rats are an example of vermin; the clue's question mark flags the definition by example

indicators.note: one thing keeping another holds it inside

blocks.note: V is the abbreviation for very
Tracey Emin was one of the Young British Artists of the 1990s; the next piece goes after her E
R is the abbreviation for river

explanation.surface: A trendy young artist keeps river rats, perhaps as an installation.
explanation.walkthrough: The Young British Artists were a 1990s art movement whose members included Damien Hirst and Tracey Emin.
explanation.definitionFit: Vermin are pest animals, and rats are the classic example.

clue.text: Manage stronghold in which I escape on foot

indicators.note: the phrase says one item sits in the preceding word, placing it inside

blocks.note: to run a business is to manage it
a fort is a fortified stronghold; the next piece goes after FOR
taken as written

explanation.surface: Someone running a fortress in which they plot a getaway on foot.
explanation.definitionFit: To run for it is an idiom meaning to flee by running, escaping on foot.

clue.text: Magnificent second place finish I achieved at the end

indicators.note: at the end points to the closing letter of the preceding word

blocks.note: S is the abbreviation for second
Pl. is the abbreviation for place, as in street names
the end is the finish
taken as written
the last letter of achieved

explanation.surface: An athlete celebrates a superb second-place finish secured at the very end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'second place finish' reads as a runner-up result; it splits into three separate pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Splendid means impressive and grand, a synonym of magnificent.

clue.text: Praise group we've left – left over the borders in Germany

indicators.note: the borders of a country are its edges, so only the outer letters are kept

blocks.note: the European Union is the group Britain left after Brexit
L is the abbreviation for left
O is the cricket abbreviation for over
the first and last letters of Germany

explanation.surface: A Brexiteer praising the decision to leave the EU, with a nod to the German frontier.
explanation.walkthrough: The British setter's 'we' is the UK, which left the European Union in 2020.
explanation.definitionFit: A eulogy is a speech or piece of writing in high praise, especially of someone who has died.
